# Education in Pakistan
Education in Pakistan follows a structured formal system inspired largely by the English educational model, beginning with pre-school (ages 3–5), continuing through primary (years 1–5), middle (years 6–8), secondary (years 9–10), and higher secondary (years 11–12) education. Primary education includes eight core disciplines such as arts, sciences, languages, mathematics, religious, and social studies, with variations in language instruction based on regional and institutional differences. Secondary education culminates in standardized exams administered by regional Boards of Intermediate and Secondary Education, leading to Secondary School Certificate (matriculation) and Higher Secondary School Certificate qualifications. Alternative qualifications such as GCE O/A Levels, IGCSE, and Advanced Placement also exist, mainly in private schools. Post-secondary education offers professional degrees in various fields and academic bachelor's, master's, and doctoral programs, though only about 6% of Pakistanis were university graduates as of 2007.
The education sector faces several challenges including limited access, gender disparities, quality concerns, and inadequate teacher training. Female enrollment and literacy rates lag behind males due to socio-cultural norms, economic barriers, and infrastructure deficits, especially in rural areas. Despite progress, gender inequality persists across educational levels. Public expenditure on education remains low (around 2% of GDP with aspirations to increase), and schools often suffer from outdated curricula and insufficient resources. Madrassas, Islamic religious schools, play a significant role, especially in underprivileged areas, sometimes emphasizing rote learning and conservative ideology. Recent public initiatives aim to improve access via distance learning and reforms in teacher education, yet systemic issues remain in ensuring relevance, quality, and equality throughout Pakistan’s education system.
